newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-Platinum prices surge on acute supply shortage.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Platinum prices surge on acute supply shortage.

text.p: Platinum and palladium prices jumped again Friday amid growing concern about an acute shortage of the metals caused by a suspension of Russian exports for five months.
"There is extreme supply tightness which has virtually brought the physical market to a halt," Refco New York analyst Tim Porter said.
Russia produces about 20 percent of the world's platinum and 60 percent of its palladium.
In the physical market, where quoted, spot platinum was indicated around $465 an ounce at the close, after seeing a morning high of $500, the highest level since 1990.

German catalytic converter maker Degussa AG warned production curbs were possible in another three to four weeks if the supply squeeze continues. Degussa produces about 20 percent of the world's catalytic converters, which are installed on cars to filter pollution from emission systems and typically use platinum or palladium.
Meanwhile, relief was unlikely from South Africa, which produces about 60 percent of the world's platinum.
"I don't believe South African producers have stocks of metal," said Barry Davison, the managing director of Amplats, the world's largest supplier.
"I don't think relief can come from here. The relief can only come from a resumption of Russian supplies and dishoarding of the metal."
German bank Dresdner on Friday called on the U.S. Defence Stockpile to release some of the 431,000 ounces of platinum and the 1.264 million ounces of palladium it holds to ease the squeeze.
But the Stockpile's manager, Peter Roman, said Thursday Congressional approval was needed for another sale and it could not be organised before the end of summer.
Earlier this year the Stockpile sold 10,000 ounces of platinum and 15,000 ounces of palladium from the U.S. strategic reserve.

Russian officials told Japanese traders Wednesday that Russian PGM exports would resume on June 20, but Friday the head of the precious metals division of Russia's Finance Ministry warned platinum group metal (PGM) exports to Japan in 1997 would be a little below the levels seen last year.
Platinum for July delivery on the New York Mercantile Exchange closed $18.30 an ounce higher at $454.90 after earlier rising to a life-of-contract high of $473.80.
NYMEX June palladium closed up $13.85 an ounce at $214.00.
Crude oil futures fell to their lowest levels since February 1996 amid rising U.S. inventories and record refinery production over the past month.
Weekly inventory reports throughout May have shown crude oil stocks 14 million barrels higher than they were at this point last year even while the nation's refineries were humming.

At the same time, the unseasonably cool spring weather in most of the nation has delayed the start of the summer "driving season," which typically boost demand for unleaded gasoline and therefore crude oil.

In addition, the United Nations earlier this week agreed to extend Iraq's "oil-for-food" deal, which renews an accord allowing Baghdad to sell up to $2.1 billion of oil over 180 days for humanitarian purposes.
Despite the low demand for gasoline, refinery production has been running at nearly full capacity.
July crude oil fell 87 cents to $18.79 a barrel on the New York Mercantile Exchange, the lowest price for the most actively traded contract in 16 months.
Prices for prompt delivery are down 30 percent this year and 15 percent in the past three weeks alone.
Refined products futures also tumbled. Unleaded gasoline fell 2.69 cents to 57.13 cents a gallon. Heating oil lost 1.80 cents, ending at 51.52 cents a gallon.
